title: Arabic coins and offices
hookLine: Arabic becomes the language of government, and coins carry verses instead of faces

lines: OLD STYLES, ARABIC AT THE EDGE.
cards: Turn a coin over in your hand. There may be a face on it: a president, a queen, a national hero. Putting a ruler's face on money is an old habit.

In the early Umayyad years, Muslim mints did much the same, striking coins in the old styles of the empires before them, with crowned figures and portraits, sometimes with a few Arabic words added at the edge.
Then the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik changed the gold and the silver. The faces went. In their place: nothing but words.

teach.h: NO GOD BUT GOD, ON GOLD.
teach.b: Look at one of the new gold coins, the dinar. In Arabic script it says: there is no god but God, alone, without partner. Around it, words from the Qur'an.
One side carries most of a short surah, al-Ikhlas, without its opening command, say, and without its last line.
In Pickthall's translation, the words on the coin read: "He is Allah, the One! Allah, the eternally Besought of all! He begetteth not nor was begotten."
A coin travels, through markets and purses from one end of the map to the other. Now it carried, not a ruler's face, but a statement about God. The same change came to the offices.
Three days ago, the clerks kept the registers in Greek in Syria and in Persian in Iraq.
The historian al-Baladhuri reports that under Abd al-Malik the registers of Syria were moved into Arabic, and under his governor al-Hajjaj the registers of Iraq were moved from Persian.
Arabic became the language of tax rolls, letters and records. That's how a language of poetry and revelation also became a language of paperwork.
Two small reforms, a coin and a ledger, changed what the money looked like and how the offices wrote.

how: Historians and coin collectors study the Umayyad reform dinars, which carry the declaration of God's oneness and verses from Surah al-Ikhlas, and al-Ikhlas is a surah recited in prayer.

games.q: you're designing the empire's new gold coin. it will pass through every market from Spain to Sindh. what goes on it?
o: the caliph's portrait, like the coins before.
words: there is no god but God, and verses of the Qur'an.
games.why: the reformed dinar carried no image at all: only Arabic words of faith, including Surah al-Ikhlas.

practice: If there's a coin nearby, pick it up, ignore the picture, and read every word on it slowly, front and back, noticing what its makers chose to say to everyone who would ever hold it. Then set it down and close your eyes.
If you pray, you can recite Surah al-Ikhlas, the words those gold coins carried; if not, simply hold the coin's words in mind.

wordCard.voice: Dinar, the gold coin of the caliphs: reformed by Abd al-Malik to carry words of faith instead of a ruler's face, alongside registers of empire moved into Arabic. Today's word.
